title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
body: In an isolated system, entropy never decreases. This explains why heat flows on its own from hot to cold, and why no engine can turn heat entirely into work.

title: Evolution by Natural Selection
body: Charles Darwin set out the theory in On the Origin of Species in 1859; Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently. Individuals with inherited traits that improve survival and reproduction pass them on, and over long periods species change.

title: The Periodic Table
body: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by atomic weight and chemical properties. He left gaps for elements not yet known and predicted their properties, which was confirmed when gallium and germanium were discovered.

title: The DNA Double Helix
body: In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick described the structure of DNA as a double helix, drawing heavily on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray images. The structure showed how genetic information can be copied.

title: Relativity
body: Einstein's special relativity of 1905 showed that measurements of time and space depend on the observer's motion, and gave the equation E = mc². General relativity, from 1915, describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

title: Photosynthesis
body: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar and oxygen. Almost all life on Earth depends on this process, and it is the source of the oxygen in the atmosphere.

title: Newton's Laws of Motion
body: In the Principia of 1687 Isaac Newton set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. They explained falling objects and planetary orbits with the same principles and underpinned physics for two centuries.

title: Heliocentrism
body: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus argued that the Earth and planets orbit the Sun. Kepler later showed that the orbits are ellipses, and Galileo's telescope observations supported the model, overturning the Earth-centred view of the cosmos.

title: Germ Theory of Disease
body: In the 19th century Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch showed that many diseases are caused by microorganisms. The theory transformed medicine, leading to antiseptic surgery, vaccines and modern public health.

title: Plate Tectonics
body: The Earth's outer shell is divided into plates that move slowly over the mantle. Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, but the theory was only accepted in the 1960s. It explains earthquakes, volcanoes and the formation of mountain ranges.

title: Penicillin
body: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould killed bacteria in his culture dish. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain later turned penicillin into a usable drug, mass-produced during the Second World War, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

title: The Big Bang
body: The universe has been expanding from an extremely hot, dense state for about 13.8 billion years. Edwin Hubble's observations in 1929 showed galaxies receding from us, and the discovery of the cosmic microwave background in 1965 strongly supported the theory.

title: The Speed of Light
body: Light travels through a vacuum at 299,792,458 metres per second. Since 1983 this value has been exact by definition, because the metre is defined from it. According to relativity, nothing with mass can reach this speed.

title: Cell Theory
body: In 1838–1839 Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed that all living things are made of cells, and Rudolf Virchow later added that every cell comes from another cell. Cell theory is one of the foundations of biology.

title: Quantum Mechanics
body: In 1900 Max Planck proposed that energy is emitted in discrete packets, or quanta. Quantum mechanics grew from this idea to describe atoms and particles, and includes Heisenberg's uncertainty principle of 1927: position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.

title: Oral Rehydration Therapy
body: Cholera and other diarrhoeal diseases kill mainly through dehydration. In the 1960s researchers in Dhaka and Calcutta showed that glucose helps the gut absorb salt and water, so a simple drink of water, salt and sugar can replace lost fluids. Used on a large scale in refugee camps during the 1971 Bangladesh war, it greatly reduced deaths and has since saved millions of lives, especially among children.

title: Newton's Prism and the Colours of Light
body: In the 1660s Isaac Newton passed sunlight through a glass prism and showed that white light is a mixture of all the colours of the spectrum. A second prism could bend a single colour but not change it, showing that the colours were not created by the glass. He published his findings in 1672 and more fully in Opticks in 1704.

title: CRISPR Gene Editing
body: CRISPR is a defence system that bacteria use to cut the DNA of invading viruses. In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that it can be programmed to cut DNA at a chosen site, making it far easier to edit genes. The technique transformed biology and medicine and raised ethical debates about altering human embryos; the two received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: Al-Tusi and the Maragha Observatory
body: In 1259 the Persian scholar Nasir al-Din al-Tusi founded an observatory at Maragha, in north-western Iran, under Mongol patronage. Astronomers there sought alternatives to Ptolemy's planetary models, and al-Tusi devised the 'Tusi couple', which produces straight-line motion from two circles. A similar device appears in Copernicus's work; whether he learned of it from Islamic sources is debated.

title: The Discovery of X-Rays
body: In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen, experimenting with cathode-ray tubes in Würzburg, discovered invisible rays that could pass through flesh but not bone. Within months doctors were using them to examine fractures and locate bullets. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901, and X-rays later revealed the structure of crystals and molecules, including DNA.

title: Radiocarbon Dating
body: In the late 1940s Willard Libby developed a method of dating once-living material by measuring its carbon-14. Living things absorb this radioactive form of carbon, and after death it decays at a known rate, halving roughly every 5,700 years. The method transformed archaeology by giving reliable ages for remains up to about 50,000 years old, and Libby received the 1960 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

title: The Eruption of Krakatoa
body: In August 1883 the volcanic island of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, was destroyed in one of the most violent eruptions in recorded history, and the tsunamis it caused killed more than 30,000 people. Its explosions were heard thousands of kilometres away, and barometers around the world recorded its pressure wave. Ash and sulphur gases thrown into the upper atmosphere caused vivid sunsets worldwide and cooled the global climate for a time; in 1888 a Royal Society report gathered observations of its effects from around the world.

title: Hutton and Deep Time
body: The Scottish geologist James Hutton argued in the 1780s that the Earth was shaped by slow processes still at work, such as erosion, deposition and uplift, acting over immense periods. Rock formations such as the tilted layers at Siccar Point convinced him that the Earth is vastly older than a few thousand years. His idea of deep time, developed by Charles Lyell, influenced Darwin.

title: Carlos Finlay and Yellow Fever
body: In 1881 the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that yellow fever is spread by a mosquito, now known as Aedes aegypti. His idea was largely ignored until 1900, when a US Army commission led by Walter Reed confirmed it in Cuba. Mosquito control then sharply reduced yellow fever, notably in Havana and during the building of the Panama Canal.

title: The Raman Effect
body: In 1928 Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman and his colleague Kariamanikkam Srinivasa Krishnan, working in Calcutta, found that when light is scattered by molecules a tiny fraction changes wavelength, revealing the molecules' vibrations. Raman spectroscopy became a standard way to identify substances. Raman received the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and India marks the discovery each year on National Science Day.

title: Catalysts and Enzymes
body: A catalyst speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, by offering a pathway that needs less energy. Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the term catalysis in 1835. Enzymes, mostly proteins, are the catalysts of living things, making possible the reactions of digestion, metabolism and DNA copying at body temperature.

title: Leeuwenhoek's Animalcules
body: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper in Delft, made tiny single-lens microscopes of remarkable power. From the 1670s he reported to the Royal Society in London that drops of water and scrapings from teeth teemed with minute creatures he called animalcules. He was the first to observe bacteria and single-celled organisms, revealing a world of life invisible to the naked eye.

title: Babylonian Astronomy
body: For centuries Babylonian scribes recorded the movements of the Moon and planets on clay tablets. In the 1st millennium BC they developed arithmetical methods to predict lunar phenomena, including eclipses, among the first mathematical astronomy anywhere. Their base-60 number system survives in the 60 minutes of an hour and the 360 degrees of a circle.

title: The Genetic Code
body: In 1961 Marshall Nirenberg and Heinrich Matthaei took the first step in cracking the genetic code, showing that RNA made only of the base U produces a chain of the amino acid phenylalanine. By the mid-1960s it was known that each sequence of three bases, a codon, specifies one of 20 amino acids or a stop signal. The code is almost the same in all living things, strong evidence of their common ancestry.

title: John Snow and Cholera
body: During a cholera outbreak in London's Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow mapped the deaths and found them clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the authorities to remove the pump's handle, arguing that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than bad air. His work is a founding example of epidemiology.

title: The Discovery of Insulin
body: In 1921 and 1922 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, in John Macleod's laboratory in Toronto and with the chemist James Collip, isolated insulin from the pancreas. Injected into a diabetic boy in January 1922, it brought his blood sugar under control. Insulin turned type 1 diabetes from a fatal disease into a manageable one, and Banting and Macleod received the 1923 Nobel Prize.

title: Archimedes' Principle
body: In the 3rd century BC Archimedes of Syracuse showed that a body immersed in a fluid is pushed upwards by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. The principle explains why ships float and balloons rise. The famous story of his discovery in the bath comes from a later Roman writer and may be legend.

title: Yukawa and the Strong Force
body: In 1935 the Japanese physicist Hideki Yukawa proposed that protons and neutrons are held together in the nucleus by a force carried by a new particle, later called the meson. He predicted its mass from the short range of the force. A particle matching his prediction, the pion, was found in 1947, and in 1949 Yukawa became the first Japanese Nobel laureate.

title: Hippocratic Medicine
body: Hippocrates of Kos, who lived in the 5th and 4th centuries BC, is regarded as the father of Western medicine. The writings attributed to him, in fact by many authors, treat illness as having natural rather than divine causes and stress careful observation of patients. The Hippocratic Oath, a pledge of medical ethics, is named after him.

title: Bose–Einstein Statistics
body: In 1924 the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose derived Planck's law of radiation by a new way of counting identical particles of light. He sent his paper to Einstein, who had it published and extended the method to atoms. Particles that follow these statistics are called bosons in his honour, and the theory predicted the Bose–Einstein condensate, first created in a laboratory in 1995.

title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
body: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in 980 and completed the Canon of Medicine in the early 11th century. It combined Greek medicine, especially Galen's, with the knowledge of physicians of the Islamic world in one systematic encyclopaedia. Translated into Latin in the 12th century, it served as a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.

title: The First Image of a Black Hole
body: Black holes, regions where gravity is so strong that not even light escapes, follow from Einstein's general relativity. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio observatories around the world acting as one Earth-sized dish, released the first image of one: a dark shadow ringed by glowing gas at the centre of the galaxy M87. In 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the heart of the Milky Way.

title: Air Pressure and the Vacuum
body: In the 1640s Evangelista Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and upended it in a dish: the column fell to a fixed height, leaving an empty space above. He concluded that the weight of the air holds the column up, and Blaise Pascal confirmed this by having the experiment repeated on a mountain, where the column was shorter. The experiments gave rise to the barometer and showed, against Aristotle, that a vacuum can exist.

title: The Asteroid That Ended the Dinosaurs
body: In 1980 a team led by Luis and Walter Alvarez reported a worldwide clay layer rich in iridium, rare on Earth but common in asteroids, at the boundary marking the dinosaurs' extinction about 66 million years ago. They proposed that a large asteroid had struck the Earth. The Chicxulub crater beneath Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula was identified as the impact site around 1990, though the role of huge volcanic eruptions is still debated.

title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus
body: This Egyptian medical text, written around 1600 BC and probably copied from older material, describes how to examine, diagnose and treat injuries such as wounds and fractures. Unlike most ancient medical writing, it relies mainly on practical treatment rather than magic. It contains some of the earliest known written descriptions of the brain.

title: The Neanderthal Genome
body: In 2010 a team led by Svante Pääbo in Leipzig published a draft genome of Neanderthals, sequenced from ancient bones. It showed that people whose ancestry lies outside Africa carry a small share, around 1 to 2%, of Neanderthal DNA, proof of interbreeding. The same year DNA from a finger bone in Siberia revealed another extinct group, the Denisovans, and Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize.

title: Absolute Zero
body: Absolute zero, 0 kelvin or −273.15 °C, is the lowest possible temperature, at which a system has the least energy it can have. In 1848 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a temperature scale starting from this point. The laws of thermodynamics imply that it can be approached ever more closely but never actually reached.

title: Maxwell's Equations
body: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell united electricity and magnetism in a single set of equations. They predicted electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light, leading Maxwell to conclude that light itself is such a wave. Heinrich Hertz produced radio waves in the late 1880s, confirming the theory that underlies radio, radar and much of modern physics.

title: Neutrino Oscillation
body: Neutrinos, ghostly particles proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930, pass through matter almost without trace. In 1998 the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan showed that neutrinos change from one type to another as they travel, which is possible only if they have mass. The Standard Model of particle physics had treated them as massless, and Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald shared the 2015 Nobel Prize.

title: The Discovery of the Electron
body: In 1897 Joseph John Thomson showed that cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles with a mass far smaller than that of the lightest atom. The electron was the first subatomic particle to be discovered, proving that atoms are not indivisible. Thomson pictured the atom as a positive sphere studded with electrons, a model soon replaced by Rutherford's.

title: Leavitt's Law and Cosmic Distances
body: Working at Harvard College Observatory, Henrietta Swan Leavitt found in 1912 that Cepheid variable stars that pulse more slowly are intrinsically brighter. Comparing a Cepheid's true brightness with how bright it appears gives its distance. Edwin Hubble used Cepheids in the 1920s to show that the Andromeda nebula lies far beyond the Milky Way, proving that other galaxies exist.

title: Galen's Medicine
body: Galen, a Greek physician of the 2nd century AD who worked in Rome, built a system of anatomy and physiology largely from dissections of animals such as apes and pigs. His writings dominated medicine in Europe and the Islamic world for well over a thousand years. Some of his errors, carried over from animal anatomy, were only corrected by Vesalius and Harvey in the 16th and 17th centuries.

title: Smallpox Inoculation
body: Long before vaccines, people in China, India, Africa and the Ottoman Empire protected themselves against smallpox by deliberately infecting healthy people with material from smallpox sores. This 'variolation' usually caused a milder illness followed by lifelong immunity, though it carried some risk. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu saw it in Constantinople and promoted it in Britain from 1721, the year it was also used in Boston on the advice of an enslaved African man, Onesimus.

title: Java Man
body: In 1891 the Dutch doctor Eugène Dubois, searching deliberately for a 'missing link', found a skullcap on the banks of the Solo River in Java, and a thigh bone the next year. They were the first known remains of the species now called Homo erectus, an early human that walked upright. It was among the first major fossil evidence for human evolution, and later finds showed that Homo erectus lived across Africa and Asia.

title: Shen Kuo's Dream Pool Essays
body: Shen Kuo, an official and scholar of China's Song dynasty, recorded a wide range of observations in his Dream Pool Essays, completed around 1088. They contain the earliest clear description of a magnetic needle compass and note that it does not point exactly south, an early recognition of magnetic declination. He also argued from fossils and silt deposits that land is formed slowly over time.

title: Harvey and the Circulation of the Blood
body: In 1628 the English physician William Harvey showed that the heart pumps blood around the body in a continuous circuit. Through experiments and a simple calculation, he showed that the heart pumps far more blood than the body could make from food, so the same blood must circulate. The tiny capillaries linking arteries and veins, which he could not see, were observed by Marcello Malpighi in 1661.

title: Humboldt's Journey Through the Americas
body: From 1799 to 1804 Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland travelled through Spanish America, measuring and collecting as they went. On the volcano Chimborazo, Humboldt observed how vegetation changes in bands with altitude, mirroring the change from the equator to the poles. His view of nature as an interconnected whole shaped biogeography and ecology and inspired Darwin.

title: The Discovery of HIV
body: AIDS was first recognised in 1981, when doctors in the United States reported rare infections in previously healthy young men. In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier at the Pasteur Institute in Paris isolated the virus responsible, later named HIV. The discovery made blood tests and antiviral drugs possible, and the two shared the 2008 Nobel Prize.
